engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Time Management
chess.body: Chess is a timed game. Use 70-80% of your clock in complex positions, blitz transitions and endgames you know. Common mistake: spending 15 minutes in the opening, then rushing in the critical middlegame. Rule: if a position is complicated and you see candidate moves, spend the time here — not in simple positions. Clock is a resource, not just a constraint.

wisdom.title: Wisdom from Fathers Before You
wisdom.body: Your father had flaws. His father did too. But they also gave you things you don't yet see. The goal isn't to be a perfect father — it's to be a slightly more conscious one. Break the patterns you don't want to pass on. Keep the ones that built you. Each generation improves a little. That's legacy.

book.author: Cal Newport
book.chapter: The Any-Benefit Mindset vs The Craftsman Mindset
book.lesson: Most people adopt the any-benefit mindset for tools: if a tool provides any benefit, use it. This is why everyone is on every social platform, attending every meeting, checking email all day. Newport argues for the craftsman mindset: identify the core factors that determine your success and happiness. Adopt a tool only if its positive impacts on these factors substantially outweigh its negative ones. Your attention is finite. Every tool that fragments it has a cost, even if it has some benefits. The question is never 'is there value here?' but 'is this the best use of my limited attention?'
book.key_quote: Your attention is your most valuable professional asset. Spend it deliberately.
book.action: List your three most important professional skills. Then ask: does checking social media or attending this meeting help or hurt those skills?
crux: Deep work: focused, undistracted, cognitively demanding work. It is becoming rare and simultaneously more valuable.
Two core abilities now decide income: learn hard things fast, and produce elite output fast.
Both abilities depend on deep work. Both are destroyed by fragmented attention.
Shallow work is logistically necessary and infinitely replaceable. It feels like work and produces nothing durable.
Attention residue: switching tasks leaves cognitive drag for 15–20 minutes. Ten switches cost you the day.
High-quality work = time spent × intensity of focus. Intensity is the neglected multiplier.
Four scheduling philosophies: monastic, bimodal, rhythmic, journalistic. Rhythmic — same hours daily — is the only one most people can sustain.
Willpower is finite and depletes. Rituals and fixed locations spend none of it.
Schedule every minute of the workday. Not to obey it, but to force the question 'what deserves this hour?'
Fixed-schedule productivity: hard-stop the day and work backwards. Constraint forces ruthless triage.
Boredom tolerance is trainable and prerequisite. If every queue is filled with a phone, focus never develops.
Quit social media by default; readmit a tool only if it clearly serves a core goal.
Drain the shallows. Aim shallow work under 40% of the week and defend the rest.
learnings: Busy is not a proxy for valuable. It is usually a proxy for unfocused.
The ability to concentrate is a skill you build, not a mood you catch.
Fragmented time is not additive — four 30-minute blocks are worth far less than one 2-hour block.
Downtime is not idleness; unconscious processing needs it.
examples: Carl Jung built a stone tower at Bollingen and wrote there in the mornings, uninterrupted, while running a clinical practice.
Adam Grant compressed teaching into one semester and batched research into the other — becoming one of the most published psychologists of his generation.
Newport wrote a book, earned a PhD, and published peer-reviewed papers while rarely working past 5:30pm, by hard-stopping his day.
adapt: One 90-minute block before 8am for the highest-leverage build. Phone in another room, not face-down on the desk.
Batch Telegram, Instagram, and email into two windows. Notifications off outside them.
Financial models are deep work. Do them before the market opens, never in gaps between messages.
Hard-stop at 7pm on weekdays. The constraint is what forces the triage.

minimalism.title: The Box Test
minimalism.body: Pack a category into a box and seal it. If you have not opened it in a month, you do not need what is inside. Most people cannot name the contents a week later.

father.title: Practise object permanence
father.do: Hide a toy under a cloth while she watches, then let her pull it off. Repeat with longer delays.
father.why: Around 7–8 months this clicks. It is also why separation anxiety starts now — she has learned you continue to exist when you leave, but not yet that you come back.

father.why: Turn-taking is the structure of conversation, learned months before words. The pause is the important part — filling it teaches her that her turn does not matter.

interview_tech.q: How does IFRS 16 change the picture for a retailer with 60 leases?
interview_tech.a: Operating leases come on balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Rent expense is replaced by depreciation plus interest, so EBITDA rises — often materially for retail — while EBIT moves little. Interest is front-loaded, so early-life leases depress net income versus the old treatment. Watch three consequences: gearing ratios jump and can breach covenants written pre-IFRS 16; EBITDA-based multiples are no longer comparable to history; and store-level return metrics need restating or you will misjudge performance.

interview_tech.q: Explain working capital optimisation to a non-finance retail board.
interview_tech.a: Working capital is cash tied up in running the business — stock on shelves and money owed to you, less money you owe suppliers. Every day of stock is cash sitting in a warehouse instead of in the bank. Frame it in days and rupees, not ratios: 'we hold 95 days of stock; every day we cut releases AED 1.1M in cash we can spend on new stores instead of borrowing.' Boards act on that. They do not act on 'DIO improved 4%.'

interview_soft.q: How do you stay current technically while managing?
interview_soft.a: Be specific and verifiable. Name the standard you last read in full and why, the technical update you attended, the thing you built yourself recently rather than delegated. Vague answers about 'reading widely' land badly with technical interviewers. The strongest version connects it to a decision: 'I went back through IFRS 16 properly when we hit the lease modification question on the Indonesian stores, and that changed how we structured the renewal.'

interview_soft.q: Where do you think retail is heading in the next five years?
interview_soft.a: Have a view and defend it with numbers, not trends. Something like: physical stores stop being judged on their own sales as fulfilment and returns blur the channels, which breaks conventional store P&L and forces a catchment-level view; margin pressure shifts from price to cost-to-serve; and in the Gulf specifically, corporate tax and e-invoicing professionalise finance functions that were previously light. Then say what you would do about it in the role you are interviewing for.

cfo_field.q: The offer is decided by the non-technical questions.
cfo_field.a: Everyone shortlisted can do the technical work — that is why they were shortlisted. What separates the offer is whether the panel believes you can hold a room, disagree with a CEO without theatre, and be trusted with bad news. Prepare the failure story properly: what you decided, what it cost, what you changed afterwards. A candidate with no failure story reads as someone who has never owned a decision.

cfo_field.q: A forecast that is never wrong is a forecast nobody is using.
cfo_field.a: Track forecast accuracy as a metric in its own right — absolute percentage error by month, by category. Under 5% at group level is good in retail; over 15% and the business has stopped believing you. But an FP&A team that is never wrong is sandbagging, and sandbagging is more expensive than error: it prices in a buffer everyone plans around, and the buffer compounds up the hierarchy.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early piece coordination: develop knights before moving the queen; aim for Nf3–d2–c4 within 5 moves to avoid queen‑side tempo losses.
Reduce blunders: before each move, verify all opponent threats and your piece safety; aim for ≤2 blunders, dropping ACPL below 30.
lichess_games.standout: 5 blunders in one game. The result is noise; the error count is the signal.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early piece coordination: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5, develop knights before pushing c‑ or d‑pawns; your 4.Bc4 allowed a quick ...Nf6‑e4 fork. Aim for solid development, avoiding premature attacks that lose tempo.

Focus on early central control: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6, play 3…Nf6 (instead of 3…Nd7) and exchange on e4 promptly; this reduces White’s space, prevents cramped Philidor structures, and improves your average centipawn loss by ~15 cp.
Focus on early piece activity: develop knights before moving the queen (e.g., avoid 4…Qb6). Aim for ≤3 % pawn‑structure damage and finish development within 8 moves.
lichess_games.standout: Over in 20 moves — decided in the opening, so the opening is what to study.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early piece activity: develop knights before bishops, castle by move 9, and avoid queen‑side pawn pushes that leave the king exposed.
Increase your opening preparation: study Philidor main lines and typical pawn structures; aim to avoid passive moves like 6…Nd7, which cost ~0.6 % accuracy each game.
lichess_games.standout: Decided on the clock, not the board — the position was still playable when time ran out.

lichess_summary.session_summary: Your opening repertoire is a joke—relying on the same generic D00 lines that give you a 33 % win rate proves you have no real preparation and leaves you vulnerable to even club‑level opponents. Stop playing “Queen’s Pawn Game” as a default; study at least two solid, theory‑backed defenses (e.g., the Caro‑Kann and the London System) and drill the critical variations until you can execute them without hesitation. From now on, analyze every loss move by move, annotate the exact moment you deviate from the main line, and add that correction to a personal opening notebook you review before every session.
